scenario.speaker: marcus
scenario.briefing:
The open-end coding is in and the topline is final — nice work on the code lists. Before Dana starts writing the report, she wants the **analysis pack**: for each research question, the right statistical test; the income cross-tab Neo's CFO asked about; the headline numbers pulled straight from the topline; and a shortlist of findings that can actually survive a client meeting.

One rule from Dana, and she means it: **every claim traces to a table.** If you can't point to the number, it doesn't go in the pack.

The memo I sent you has the topline funnel attached. Work through the four pages in order — the test choices first, because everything else depends on asking the data the right way.

inbox.subject: Analysis pack — topline funnel attached
inbox.body:
Four jobs in this one:

1. **Test selection.** Four research questions from the proposal, each needing the right analysis. Use the level-of-measurement logic — what kind of variable is on each side of the question?
2. **Income cross-tab.** The CFO wants to know what's different about the $100K+ households (n = 166). Same rule as always: flag a row only when the segment mean is at or above the overall mean.
3. **Topline reads.** Three numbers Dana will say out loud in the client meeting. Pull them exactly — she does not round in front of clients.
4. **Defensible findings.** Six candidate claims are circulating from the team. Only three trace to a table. Pick those three.

The funnel table is attached. The cross-tab data is on its page.

— Marcus

guides.title: From Research Question to Test
guides.body:
**The test is chosen by the variables, not by preference.** Identify the level of measurement on each side of the research question, then read off the analysis:

| This side | That side | Analysis |
|---|---|---|
| Categorical (2 groups) | Interval/ratio (a mean) | Independent samples t-test |
| Categorical | Categorical | Cross-tab + two-way chi-square |
| Continuous | Continuous | Correlation (then simple regression) |
| One categorical variable | — | Descriptive frequencies + sorted bar |

Two habits that prevent most errors: (1) say each variable out loud with its type before choosing — "HOA status: categorical, two groups; likelihood: 1–5 rating, treated as interval"; (2) when a rating scale is on one side, resist the urge to chi-square it — binning a 1–5 rating into categories throws information away.

Round pointer: all four research questions on this page use variables you have already met in the topline. The cheat-sheet logic decides every one of them.

guides.title: Reading a Cross Tabulation
guides.body:
**A cross-tab sets a segment's result next to the total sample's.** The working rule: compare the segment mean to the overall mean, row by row. At or above → the segment over-indexes; below → it under-indexes. Both directions are findings — a segment that worries LESS about cost is exactly as informative as one that likes a concept more.

Discipline points: the comparison is mechanical, so do not narrate yourself out of a row that is 0.05 above the overall mean — at or above means at or above. And keep the base sizes in view: a segment of n = 166 is plenty for means, but sub-slicing it further is where cross-tabs quietly fall apart.

Round pointer: the CFO's question is about the $100K+ households. Expect the interesting rows to run in BOTH directions — what they want more of, and what worries them less.
